title: Like, here's the episode on "like"
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the word "like" in English: its Old English roots (geliched, leich, the -lich suffix), the five accepted grammatical uses (verb, noun, preposition, conjunction, suffix), and the conversational functions linguists have named: quotative complementizer, approximate adverb, discourse marker, and discourse particle/softener/hedge. They cover the Valley Girl stereotype, the Frank Zappa "Valley Girl" song and 1982-83 movies, earlier bebop/jive-talk usage, and research by Alexandra D'Arcy and others finding gender and age differences in how "like" is used. They argue that criticism of the word is often coded sexism or ageism. The episode closes with a listener email about The Simpsons Clue board game.

segments.title: Opening banter on the word like
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on the word 'like' and note that people both use it and object to it.

segments.title: Etymology of like
segments.summary: Origins of 'like' from Old English geliched (with the body of, similar to), the -lich suffix becoming -ly, and the verb sense of 'to be pleasing' (the music likes you not, from Shakespeare). Older uses such as 'nearly' in the 17th century are mentioned.

segments.title: Five accepted grammatical uses of like
segments.summary: The hosts list the widely accepted uses of 'like': verb, noun, preposition (looks like), conjunction (like I always said), and suffix (childlike versus childish). Ish is briefly mentioned as a related suffix.

segments.title: Slang like and its critics
segments.summary: Hosts discuss listeners who object to slang 'like' and the claim that it is meaningless or destroys English, and introduce the Jordans mall script used to illustrate the functions.

segments.title: Quotative like
segments.summary: The quotative complementizer sets up a paraphrase or impression of what someone said, signaling approximate rather than exact quotation. Sammy Davis Jr. is given as an example of mimicry.

segments.title: Approximate adverb like
segments.summary: Like used to mean roughly or about, as in 'two hundred and fifty dollars,' and 'I have like one hundred pairs of shoes,' citing research by Jones, Zaane and Engrossman (2022). The word hedges exact numbers.

segments.title: Discourse marker like
segments.summary: Like as a discourse marker, a traffic signal in spoken English (Kurzan). Its functions include signaling exaggeration, elaboration, and emphasis or surprise, which depends on tone.

segments.title: Discourse particle like as softener and hedge
segments.summary: Like as a discourse particle softens criticism and shields feelings, and also hedges the speaker's own claims. D'Arcy and John McWhorter are cited; studies suggest speech without such particles sounds robotic.

segments.title: History of like and Valley Girls
segments.summary: Valley Girls are commonly credited with popularizing 'like', helped by Frank Zappa's 1982 song 'Valley Girl' with Moon Zappa and the 1983 movie. Like was already in use earlier, in bop, jive and Beat slang and in 19th-century England. The quotative use is the one that seems to have emerged in the 1980s.

segments.title: Sexism and ageism in criticism of like
segments.summary: Blaming young women for 'infecting' the language is called factually inaccurate and sexist. Research by D'Arcy and Kinsler finds men and women use like at similar rates overall, with differences by function and age. Greta Thunberg is cited as an example of dismissive treatment of young women.

segments.title: Conclusion on whether like is harmful
segments.summary: Hosts conclude that critics do not have a linguistic point, since like fills conversational functions no other word fills, and it signals inclusion and acknowledgment in speech.

segments.title: Listener mail: Simpsons Clue
segments.summary: Listener Margaret Nihawk writes about receiving The Simpsons Clue board game, describing its characters, weapons, and locations.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck asks listeners to get in touch by email, and the hosts close the show.
